summary: An overview of a 2002 workshop held by the Internet Architecture Board on network management, in Reston, Virginia. The workshop continued a dialog between network operators and protocol developers and was meant to guide future management work in the IETF. It is informational.

eli5.summary: This is a report on a meeting where the people who run networks told the people who design the rules what they needed, so the rules would help more.

subtitle: A report on the 2002 meeting where network operators told the IAB what network management tools were missing.

tldr.problem: Operators said that IETF network management work, especially for configuration, did not address their real needs.
tldr.mechanism: The IAB held an invitational workshop in Reston, Virginia, compared management technologies, listed operator requirements and SNMP shortcomings, and agreed recommendations.
tldr.outcome: The report recommends focusing on configuration management and XML-based configuration, and not on HTML or HTTP-based methods.

today: RFC 3535 is an Informational RFC and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is a record of the workshop's views and recommendations as of 2002.

sections.title: Why the Workshop Happened
sections.content:
The Internet Architecture Board held an invitational workshop on network management hosted by CNRI in Reston, VA, from June 4 to June 6, 2002. During 2001, meetings at NANOG-22, RIPE-40, LISA-XV and IETF-52 started a direct dialog between operators and protocol developers. Several operators said that IETF developments did not address their requirements, especially for configuration management.

The goal was to continue that dialog and to guide the IETF's focus on future work. The main IETF technologies of the time were SNMP (RFC 3410), the policy extensions of the Common Information Model (PCIM, RFC 3060), and COPS-PR (RFC 3084), which extends COPS (RFC 2748) to provision configuration.
sections.eli5: Network operators complained that the tools did not help them do their jobs. So a group met for three days to figure out what to fix.

sections.title: Strengths and Weaknesses of Six Technologies
sections.content:
Breakout sessions listed strong and weak points of six technologies: SNMP with MIBs, COPS-PR with PIBs, CIM, command line interfaces over TELNET and SSH, HTTP and HTML, and XML.

  • SNMP works reasonably well for monitoring, but standard MIBs often lack writable objects, it is slow for large data such as routing tables, and it has no easy retrieval and playback of configurations.
  • COPS-PR has well-defined transactions and rollback, but at the time there were no standardized PIB modules and not enough operational experience.
  • CIM is object-oriented and uses UML, but interoperability between implementations seemed problematic and it had seen limited use between management systems and devices.
  • CLI is task-oriented and easy to replay as text, but lacks a common data model and is hard to parse programmatically.
  • HTTP and HTML are friendly to end users, but hostile to management applications.
  • XML is machine readable with good tools, but verbose, and there was a lack of accepted management-specific schemas.
sections.eli5: Each tool is like a different kind of key. Some are easy for people, some are easy for computers, and none opened every door.

sections.title: What Operators Asked For
sections.content:
Operators listed 14 needs. Ease of use came first. Others included a clear distinction between configuration data, operational state and statistics, and the ability to fetch each separately. They asked for configuration transactions across several devices, a way to compute the operations needed to get from configuration A to B with minimal effect, and standard ways to dump and restore configurations.

They also wanted text tools such as diff, RCS and CVS to work on configurations, which means devices should not reorder data such as access control lists arbitrarily. They asked for role-based access control with least privilege, consistency checks of access control lists across devices, separation of distributing a configuration from activating it, and support for both data-oriented and task-oriented access control. The report notes that no published document clearly defined operator requirements at that point.
sections.eli5: Operators said: make it easy, let us save and restore settings, let us undo a change safely, and give each person only the keys they need.

sections.title: SNMP Framework Criticisms
sections.content:
The workshop recorded 20 properties of the SNMP framework. Among them: complete device configurations usually cannot be retrieved, the quality of SNMP instrumentation is sometimes disappointing, and MIB modules sometimes lag years behind. Operators found scripting interfaces too low-level, bulk transfers and unanticipated queries performed poorly, and credential and key management was considered complex.

Others noted that the SMI language is hard to deal with, MIB modules are often over-engineered, and traps often need follow-up get operations while syslog messages carry more information. The report also says SNMP seems to work reasonably well for small devices, but for more complex devices it becomes too expensive and too hard to use. The consolidated observations add that eliminating SNMP altogether is not an option, and that textual configuration files should use UTF-8.
sections.eli5: SNMP is good at checking on small devices, but it is awkward for changing settings on big ones. Even so, nobody wanted to throw it away.

sections.title: Recommendations to the IETF
sections.content:
The workshop made eight recommendations. Among them, with strong consensus from both operators and protocol developers, the IETF should focus resources on standardizing configuration management mechanisms. With strong consensus from operators and rough consensus from developers, the IETF and IRTF should spend resources on XML-based device configuration and management technologies, and should not spend resources on HTML-based or HTTP-based methods.

Other recommendations: stop forcing working groups to provide writable MIB modules, form groups to investigate why MIB modules and SNMP do not meet monitoring needs, continue evolving the SMI and SPPI languages in the SMIng working group, and work on fixing the MIB development process. The workshop also reached rough consensus, without a formal recommendation, that the IETF should not spend resources on CIM extensions, COPS-PR development or SPPI PIB definitions.
sections.eli5: The main advice was: work on easy, safe ways to configure devices, use XML for it, and stop spending effort on web-page style controls.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The report says that, as a record of a workshop, it has no direct security implications for the Internet. Security does appear in the discussions it summarizes: operators asked for robust access control, and the consolidated observations call for secure transport, authentication, identity and access control that integrate with existing key and credential management infrastructure.
sections.eli5: The report itself cannot hurt anyone, but the people at the meeting did ask for better locks on management tools.
